articles.title: Three Bob Fergusons and two JFKs: A brief history of same-name ballot shenanigans
articles.summary: Before there were two Dan Sullivans, there were three Bob Fergusons.
articles.body:
Before there were two Dan Sullivans, there were three Bob Fergusons.

In 2024, Washington's Democratic state Attorney General Bob Ferguson was joined in the gubernatorial primary race by two other Democratic hopefuls with the same name.

Was it a coincidence? More like an age-old election trick that's come up again in this year's tightly contested Alaska US Senate race .

In Washington two years ago, a Republican activist had paid the other two Bob Fergusons to run in the hopes that their names on the ballot would confuse voters — an effort to weaken the attorney general's candidacy. But the decoys ultimately dropped out after just a few days when the first Bob Ferguson, who went on to be elected governor, threatened legal action and publicly derided their candidacy as an "attack on our democracy."

Now the tables have turned with Republicans accusing Democrats of a similar ploy in Alaska. A New York Times story Wednesday revealed that Democrats appeared to be behind having a potential Republican spoiler candidate, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, siphon votes from incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The Justice Department has preemptively sued to block the results if the incumbent loses. Both Alaska and DOJ are investigating , and President Donald Trump has called for the criminal prosecution of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, writing in a Truth Social post that she should "suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done."

"So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan," Trump wrote. "Nothing else will do!"

But there's a long history of political operatives from both parties deploying the tactic — and largely getting away with it.

"It's a time-honored tradition," said Thomas Kahn, director of the Center for Congressional and Presidential Studies at American University.

"It's not a good practice," Kahn added, but "if trying to confuse voters was a crime, then every politician would be in jail."

One century-old example of same-name ballot stacking came in the 1930 Nebraska Republican US senate primary, when incumbent George W. Norris was dismayed to suddenly see another George W. Norris, a grocery clerk, running. "I'm finished unless the other George W. Norris is kept off the ballot," the incumbent senator said at the time .

It was ultimately a technicality that spoiled the candidacy for the spoiler grocer. Just as Sen. Norris prepared to withdraw from the Republican primary and run as an independent, the chief justice of the Nebraska Supreme Court ruled that the other Norris was ineligible because his petition had not been legally filed in time.

Perhaps no other same-name candidate was more opportunistic than the "other JFK." Rather than a decoy deployed by the opposite party, John Francis Kennedy, a Gillette razor factory stockroom supervisor, was a private citizen who merely capitalized on the Massachusetts name recognition of then-Sen. John Fitzgerald Kennedy. John Francis filed for state treasurer in 1954 and won without any party endorsement or public campaigning.

The high school dropout from South Boston went on to win three terms. During his 1956 reelection bid, he was challenged by another political newcomer who entered the race because he was outraged that someone would pirate the good name of the Massachusetts senator. That candidate's name was John M. Kennedy.

Simply possessing the same name as a candidate is constitutionally protected under ballot access rules. Criminality occurs when operatives cross into falsifying residency documents, laundering campaign funds or offering direct payments in exchange for filing.

That was the case in Florida in 2020. Authorities claimed that Republican state Sen. Frank Artiles recruited "ghost candidate" Alex Rodriguez with a $50,000 payment to run for office in the Florida legislature and to cause the Democratic incumbent with the same surname, Jose Javier Rodriguez, to lose the election by taking votes away in the razor-thin race. Alex Rodriguez received over 6,000 votes in the election, and Republican candidate Ileana Garcia beat the incumbent by just 32 votes.

Artiles was ultimately convicted of excessive campaign contributions and procuring the falsification of a candidate oath form. Alex Rodriguez had sworn that he lived in the district's limits when he actually resided in another county.

While Florida law permits ghost candidates but prohibits people making excessive amounts of campaign contributions over $1,000, Bob Ferguson leaned on an 81-year-old Washington state law that makes it a felony to challenge someone with the same name "and whose political reputation is widely known, with intent to confuse and mislead the electors" to get the other two Bob Fergusons to drop their candidacies after just 72 hours when he threatened legal action.

In Alaska, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said in a post on X that he would investigate if the "scheme" of recruiting a second Dan Sullivan to run "violated Alaska's laws." The Department of Justice last week preemptively filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska's US Senate election if the incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, asking the court to potentially delay the certification of the election if the incumbent is defeated but would have won if "all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan" had "been cast instead for Senator Sullivan."

Legal experts have said the suit is unlikely to succeed. The state's Supreme Court already ruled to keep the retired teacher on the ballot and Alaska's Division of Elections sought to differentiate between the two Sullivans by listing the senator as the incumbent Republican and the other without a party affiliation.

Alaska's top-four primary election process — where the top four vote-getters advance to the general election regardless of their partisan affiliations — and ranked-choice voting system make the state particularly susceptible to same-name and spoiler candidate hijinks. The ranked-choice system, however, allows voters to show a preference for more than one candidate, so even if voters were hypothetically confused about which Dan Sullivan to vote for, they could select both, which would still favor the incumbent senator over Peltola.

The August primary for Alaska's Senate seat saw multiple efforts to boost minor candidates to hurt Peltola or the incumbent Sullivan. One group, Fair Deal Alaska, spent more than $800,000 attacking Peltola while promoting a lesser-known Democratic candidate and a Green Party candidate. A post-primary campaign finance filing revealed the group was mostly funded by the Senate Leadership Fund, the top GOP super PAC in Senate races.

And in 2024, Alaska's Democratic Party sued to keep someone off the US House ballot: Eric Hafner, who has no apparent ties to the state and is serving time in a federal prison in New York. The Democratic Party argued that it and its preferred candidate — ironically, Peltola — would be harmed because having an unaffiliated Democrat on the ballot "would confuse voters."

A divided state Supreme Court allowed Hafner to remain on the ballot. He is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the November 3 ranked vote general election ballot.

CNN's Patrick Svitek contributed reporting.

articles.title: Ponte Presidente Dutra: Trânsito melhora após retirada de caminhão | G1
articles.standfirst: Veículo estava preso no trecho em Juazeiro (BA) e provocou congestionamento no sentido Petrolina (PE). Orla da cidade ficou travada, e travessia por barquinha registrou filas enormes.
articles.summary: Após a retirada de um caminhão na Ponte Presidente Dutra pela PRF, o trânsito em Petrolina e a travessia por barquinhas começam a normalizar de forma gradual.
articles.body:
Um caminhão que ficou preso neste sábado (31), na descida da Ponte Presidente Dutra, em Juazeiro (BA), foi liberado, conforme informações da Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF). A ocorrência provocou congestionamento em Petrolina , no Sertão de Pernambuco, afetando o trânsito na cidade.

A Orla de Petrolina ficou travada, enquanto a travessia por barquinha registrou filas enormes, com embarcações lotadas.

Após a liberação do trecho, o fluxo de veículos começou a ser restabelecido, e o trânsito apresenta melhora. Apesar disso, a normalização deve ocorrer de forma gradual, já que ainda há congestionamento acumulado nos trechos afetados.

articles.summary: A falta de água em Belém afeta bairros como Jurunas e Nazaré após a Águas do Pará adiar a conclusão de reparos na rede de abastecimento neste sábado.
articles.body:
Torneira sem água. — Foto: Pedro França/Agência Senado

Mais de 15 bairros de Belém seguem sem água na tarde deste sábado (31). A manutenção no sistema de abastecimento, iniciada na noite de sexta-feira (30) , precisou ser estendida , segundo a Águas do Pará.

Por volta das 17h30, a Águas do Pará informou que o conserto do vazamento de água, em tubulação de grande porte, foi finalizado na tarde deste sábado (31).

"A distribuição de água já foi reiniciada e o sistema está recuperando aos poucos para que a água volte a ter força nas tubulações", informou a empresa.

Segundo a empresa, mesmo após as manobras de fechamento, o fluxo de água na tubulação impediu a conclusão da manutenção no prazo previsto.

Os trabalhos incluem a substituição de equipamentos e o reparo de um vazamento na rede.

articles.title: Acidentes contra postes deixam mais de 11 mil clientes sem energia | G1
articles.standfirst: Em outubro, 131 colisões foram registradas na região, quase 11 vezes mais que no mesmo mês de 2025. Em caso de colisão, motoristas e passageiros devem permanecer no veículo e aguardar as equipes de socorro.
articles.summary: O número de acidentes envolvendo postes de energia elétrica disparou na região de Presidente Prudente (SP) em outubro.
articles.body:
Acidentes contra postes prejudicam fornecimento de energia e colocam em risco a segurança das pessoas — Foto: Divulgação/Energisa

O número de acidentes envolvendo postes de energia elétrica disparou na região de Presidente Prudente (SP) em outubro. Conforme balanço divulgado pela Energisa nesta sexta-feira (30), foram 131 ocorrências neste mês, quase 11 vezes mais do que no mesmo período de 2025 , quando a concessionária registrou 12 casos .

Como consequência dessas colisões, neste mês mais de 11,2 mil clientes tiveram o fornecimento de energia interrompido temporariamente , enquanto no ano passado, 587 clientes foram afetados.

Com o feriado prolongado de Finados, a concessionária ainda alerta para os riscos desse tipo de colisão, que pode provocar interrupções no fornecimento de energia e colocar vidas em perigo.

Dependendo da intensidade da batida, os estragos podem atingir postes, cabos, transformadores e outros equipamentos, exigindo uma operação especializada para recuperar a estrutura e restabelecer o fornecimento de energia, conforme Maurício Arantes, coordenador do Centro de Operação Integrado (COI) da concessionária.

“O sistema elétrico conta com equipamentos modernos que permitem realizar procedimentos automáticos para restabelecer a energia mais rapidamente para o maior número possível de clientes. Mas nem sempre é possível normalizar o fornecimento para todos de uma só vez. Dependendo da complexidade dos danos, os reparos podem demandar mais tempo e, por questões de segurança, os trabalhos precisam ser realizados com a rede desligada”, explica Maurício.

Além dos prejuízos ao fornecimento de energia, as colisões ameaçam a segurança das pessoas. O choque elétrico é o risco mais grave, principalmente quando o poste cai sobre o veículo ou há rompimento de cabos.

Por esse motivo, Mauricio reforça algumas orientações importantes para quem se envolver ou presenciar uma colisão contra poste : motorista e passageiros devem manter a calma e permanecer dentro do veículo, sem tocar nas partes metálicas, aguardando a chegada das equipes de socorro e da concessionária.

Quem estiver do lado de fora também não deve se aproximar do carro, do poste ou de fios caídos, nem tentar prestar socorro sem os cuidados necessários.

“Mesmo que a rede de distribuição tenha equipamentos de proteção capazes de interromper automaticamente o fornecimento de energia em determinadas situações de falha, não se pode descartar o risco de choque elétrico. A rede pode continuar energizada, por isso é fundamental manter distância e aguardar a chegada de profissionais preparados para atender a ocorrência”, alerta o coordenador.

A orientação é acionar imediatamente o Corpo de Bombeiros, pelo telefone 193, e a distribuidora de energia, pelo aplicativo Energisa ON ou pelo Call Center 0800 70 10 326.

articles.title: Greg Abbott’s Texas Empire Is Showing Cracks
articles.summary: The country’s longest-serving governor is trying to keep the GOP together to notch another victory.
articles.body:
HOUSTON, Texas — On the first day of early voting in Texas, two weeks before the most consequential election Texas Republicans have faced in a generation, Greg Abbott addressed a sweaty crowd of hundreds of supporters packed inside an imitation saloon. The Texas governor pulled out a piece of paper from his pocket.

"Steve Radack Community Center, 18650 Clay Road, Houston, 1.2 miles away," he read, identifying the precinct's nearest polling location. "Listen, I can roll over there in five minutes," said Abbott, who uses a wheelchair, as the fawning audience laughed.

Abbott was making a closing pitch to the Republican Party's most fanatic supporters, many donning "Make America Texas" hats, who clapped loudly as he bragged about bringing 2.6 million jobs to Texas and booed at the mention of his "crazy" opponent, Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. And they perked up when Abbott asked if they wanted to "be your own political power broker and make sure that you're the one responsible for us winning."

That's when the governor issued another set of directions: Download the Abbott Impact App, the engine of the massive turnout operation that has enabled the GOP to build tremendous power over Abbott's nearly 12 years in Austin. Many in the audience dutifully complied. The app is the key to Abbott's ability to maintain his grip on the most influential red state in the nation through his extensive data, polling and "get out the vote" operation — powerful tools that have not only allowed him to sail to reelection repeatedly but has cemented GOP control of every single statewide office.

That could all change in a matter of days.

Abbott expected to spend 2026 in legacy mode, cruising to a fourth term that would carry him into the post-Trump era as one of the most dominant state-level GOP figures in America, a kingmaker in a party looking for new heroes. Instead, he's fighting a tougher-than-expected battle to retain his own seat, under weight from the unpopular war in Iran and rural blowback to data centers, Flock cameras and school vouchers.

His longtime ticketmate, Attorney General Ken Paxton, is facing an even more arduous challenge in his attempt to keep the state's U.S. Senate seat in Republican hands. A victory by Democrat James Talarico would crack a three-decade lockout from power in Texas for his party, and potentially redraw the national map ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Texas Republicans who have lost confidence in Paxton as a candidate, and are worried about the sour national mood more broadly, are now banking on Abbott's finely tuned, expansive GOTV political machine to save the party.

Ultimately, the election will reveal whether even the most powerful political force in Texas can fall — and determine what becomes of the Texas GOP if voters deliver a blow to the heart of American conservatism.

"Paxton's going to win the race," Abbott told reporters in Austin in October as he kicked off a mad campaigning dash across the state, in response to being asked by POLITICO Magazine who gets the blame should Paxton lose. "So the real question is who gets the credit for it."

Not long ago there was a time when Abbott could clearly claim such credit. There's arguably no Republican in America who has done more to nurture and benefit from the populist MAGA energy that President Donald Trump has unleashed over the past decade than Abbott. He has been able to navigate the yawning divisions between the two wings of the GOP by carefully riding the rise of the far right while also maintaining the respect of old school country club Republicans. That formula didn't work for Sen. John Cornyn, who found himself on the wrong side of MAGA a few too many times to maintain the fragile marriage of GOP factions and was ousted by Paxton in this year's primary. Yet Abbott has deftly managed the party's splintering, perhaps better than any other Republican whose rise pre-dated Trump.

The question now is whether he can still motivate the base with the same intensity he's done again and again. Even though most Texas Republicans — and many Democrats as well — quickly dismiss the scenario that Abbott himself could lose, public polling consistently shows Hinojosa within striking distance.

Abbott has alienated rural voters over his staunch support for data centers and school vouchers , while his ties to megabillionaires have fueled a Democratic campaign that casts the election as a referendum on corruption as much as affordability. Meanwhile, some establishment Republicans have grown weary of the party's fixation on culture-war battles that Abbott himself has helped stoke, particularly in an election where voters say they care more about the economy. It remains to be seen whether Abbott's GOTV operation can surge turnout despite those headwinds.

"He was the coattails for every cycle as governor," said a senior Republican Texas official, granted anonymity to speak freely about the state's dominant GOP leader. "He got people over the finish line in difficult House seats and Senate seats and congressional seats. He was the man."

This cycle, the official said, "Abbott has no coattails."

Texans of both parties say they've seen this scenario before: An abrasive, flamethrowing Republican is in the fight of his political life against a charismatic, rising-star Democrat who has reignited the party's hopes of ending their decades-long losing streak in Texas by flipping a Senate seat.

Faced with the limitations of his own ground game, the Republican leans on Abbott's massive field operation to churn out votes, an organization powered by an army of thousands of volunteers and advanced data metrics.

In 2018, Abbott's operation helped Ted Cruz beat Beto O'Rourke by about 219,000 votes, running up the score in rural areas and turning out unreliable Republican voters. Cruz's team saw the gap in the data: Abbott had a far broader coalition and a statewide field team that could help Republicans weather the unprecedented Democratic turnout O'Rourke was driving. The governor easily won his race by 13 points.

"He's feared because of a very effective organization," said Bill Noble, a former senior adviser to Abbott's predecessor, former Texas GOP Gov. Rick Perry. "It's better to be on the side of having the governor endorsing you, and with that endorsement comes more than just a press release. Money's made available, lists and resources are made available [and] delivering the vote after the endorsement."

Abbott's hope is that the 2018 magic that saved Cruz can play out in the final years of the Trump era for Paxton, even with his party in transition. But the barriers facing the GOP — and Abbott himself — are far stronger this time around.

Sure, Abbott can give Paxton a ground game. But can he turn Abbott voters into Paxton voters? And more to the point: Are there as many Abbott voters as there were in 2018?

Meanwhile, after decades of being outgunned by Republicans, Democrats are working on building their own turnout machine.

Brazoria County is the blueprint. Stretching from Houston to the Gulf Coast, this county has been run almost entirely by Republicans since the Republic of Texas was established in 1836. It's the former political home base of the libertarian-leaning Republican Ron Paul and hotbed of the Tea Party movement before its reactionary politics went national in 2010.

Therefore the odds are daunting for the small group of Democrats who, in 2025, devised a plan to mount a coordinated campaign within Brazoria County to assemble strength from the bottom up. The Brazoria project grew out of a statewide coordinated campaign launched this year by a coalition of Democratic groups who have invested $30 million in an effort to end the party's 30-year drought in winning higher office. The experiment is targeting Brazoria this midterm and if successful, Democrats plan to replicate it across the state the next cycle.

Texas Democrats have long yearned for year-round, state-wide campaign infrastructure. That burden typically falls on the Democrat at the top of the ticket to build out themselves, as in 2018 when O'Rourke created a massive, decentralized GOTV operation that relied on armies of volunteers. But after he lost, it evaporated. This cycle's statewide coordinated campaign running in tandem with the Brazoria project intends to copy-and-paste that strategy but in a permanent way that will exist after the fumes of the 2026 election dissipate.

Democrats believe the ingredients in Brazoria are all there, a microcosm of the story of Texas' demographic growth over the last decade. Over the past 15 years, new residents from both inside and outside Texas have poured into the region, drawn by good schools, plentiful jobs and proximity to a major city — and by the promise of planting roots in the massive master-planned communities that have become a hallmark of Texas living.

Brazoria's growth is reshaping not just its suburbs but its demographics. Hispanic residents now make up about 32% of the county's population, while Black residents account for roughly 18% and Asian residents nearly 9%. Those demographics work in Democrats' favor: Enraged by ICE's aggressive immigration enforcement under Trump, Latino voters are rapidly moving away from the GOP after a record number of them supported the president in 2024.

But Texas Democrats are learning that demographics alone won't deliver them power without some grit.

The idea, Texas Majority PAC's Katherine Fischer said, was to borrow from Republicans' 1980s playbook: invest in rural, Democratic-leaning counties that were beginning to trend Republican — just the reverse. Brazoria caught their attention as they observed it shifting bluer cycle after cycle, although Democratic gains stalled slightly in 2024 when Trump won it by 20 points. They wanted to accelerate that shift, starting by recruiting a full slate of candidates for the first time.

Republicans have so dominated the state's politics that Democrats in the past didn't even bother to field candidates in many down-ballot races. The Texas Democratic Party and Texas Majority PAC decided to fill every seat in Brazoria and partnered with County Democratic Chair Monica Morgan to make that happen. Those groups poured $450,000 into the project — hiring staff, paying for an office and covering the thousands of dollars in filing fees that dissuades potential candidates from making the leap.

Candidates were then given one-on-one training through Texas Majority PAC, which provided campaign strategy, fundraising support, voter-data guidance and canvassing help. "[The PAC is] really pushing us in a healthy way to be successful," said Becky Singleton, a Democrat running for county commissioner. "It took my own campaign to a whole new level."

The slate of Brazoria Democrats, who have become close friends throughout the cycle, got an early jolt of inspiration: In May, Democrat Quentin Wiltz flipped Brazoria's biggest city of Pearland, winning by 263 votes in a city of about 130,000. For them it was a sign that Democrats had a chance to prevail, even in a county Trump carried by a wide margin.

"We have millions of people in Texas who historically have been under-engaged," Wiltz said. "When you give people a reason to participate and organize, and then when you have the resources to invest in them, you can reach them and you can see the change that's possible."

Brazoria Republicans, in the face of a real opposition this year, are digging in. They're even consolidating behind a deceased judicial candidate who died in September. Should the candidate win next week, the GOP-controlled board of county commissioners will appoint his replacement. (The Democrat in the race, Shenequa Harrison, makes the case that "if you vote for him, you literally you don't know who you're voting for.")

Democrats' ambition now is to scale this model dramatically, with organizers saying they could recruit and support three times as many local candidates next cycle.

"If we see that the experiment in Brazoria seems to be successful, we can then export that experiment to other counties across the state," Fischer said, pointing to rapidly growing Kaufman County outside Dallas and the heavily Hispanic Rio Grande Valley as potential next targets.

"We're not going to win overnight, but we will win one day, and we want to speed it up and make sure that we have good people in these seats when we do actually win."

Many Texas Republicans see Abbott's GOTV dominance as an expression of his reputation as a hardworking overachiever with an intense obsession with detail. That reputation is in part a result of his biography: As a 26-year-old law firm associate studying for the bar, he was out for a jog when in a freak accident, a tree fell on him, leaving the lower half of his body paralyzed. The accident didn't halt his meteoric rise from attorney to judge to state attorney general to governor. "He's tenacious," GOP state Sen. Paul Bettencourt said. "Incredibly disciplined," said Republican state Rep. Greg Bonnen. "He has overcome a tremendous amount of adversity," state Sen Phil King said.

Abbott's campaign knew that this would be a tough election year, so his aides adjusted their GOTV strategy. "We increased the targets and we increased the universe," Dave Carney, Abbott's top political adviser, told me. Rather than begin canvassing immediately after the primary, as it had during his previous reelection bid, the team held back its volunteers until the fall, betting that voter contact would be more effective once the race was on voters' radar.

Those volunteers — about 10,000 — have identified 3 million potential voters through the Abbott Impact App by uploading their contacts and matching them to voter files to confirm party affiliation and determine if they have voted. The app gamifies voter outreach, which occurs either through text or door knocks, and rewards top users with prizes like a Traeger grill, Dyson blowdryer or private tour of the governor's mansion. "It's basically a field operation on your phone," Carney said.

Abbott's team insists they're still focused on the governor's goal of flipping seats in Harris County, which includes Houston and has a history of swinging between parties although it is currently Democratic-run. Abbott has devoted more than $30 million of his war chest to the effort. In 2024 Republicans successfully flipped several Harris judicial races and this year they're eyeing races toward the top of the ballot like county judge — which would amount to an exceptional coup in a difficult year.

"Any vote we pull out of Harris County is going to help the statewide ticket," said Jessica Colon, Abbott's senior adviser running the field operation in Harris County. "If it's a voter numbers contact game, we've got 'em smashed with that," said Jeff MacGeorge, a district field director in Harris County, who said his team has sent more than 3.5 million texts to voters since the primary and 2,000 people in the county have downloaded the app.

Republican state Rep. Gary Gates, who represents a district in the Houston area, said he opens the Abbott Impact App every Monday morning to see how many blocks the governor's volunteers walked the weekend before, efforts the four-term Republican says he has never seen as organized or extensive. In one week in October the Abbott team knocked on more than 5,300 doors and completed 1,300 voter surveys in his Fort Bend County district, he said.

But even with those efforts, Gates is pessimistic about how Republicans will fare next week given the negative national environment. After all, knocking on a voter's door does not ensure they will show up at the polls for your side.

"You just can't go tick off and declare war on the Latinos and not have it come back and bite you in the rear end," Cates said. "That's going to have consequences."

Early vote returns signaled some warning signs for Republicans, with Democrats showing up in slightly higher numbers while rural voter turnout is lagging . Of course, those dynamics can quickly reverse, a possibility Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows is betting on, thanks largely to Abbott. "Many of them believe Election Day is the right day to vote," he said. "So I expect us to have a huge Election Day for Republicans."

Burrows was doing his part, participating in a cross-state bus tour to mobilize Republicans: "It feels really good on the ground," he told me. "It feels a whole lot better than what it sounds like on Twitter."

That confidence in the rural firewall is not shared among all Republicans, particularly with Abbott's biggest detractors within the party. Former GOP state Rep. Glenn Rogers — whom Abbott successfully chased from office in his vendetta against lawmakers who opposed his school voucher push — said he's had many conversations with Republicans in his small town of Graford indicating slipping support for the governor. Abbott's efforts to attract data centers to Texas — which he dialed back following backlash — coupled with private school advocacy has alienated those supporters and promoted a "distrust" of him, Glenn said. A Republican defeat next week might trigger a recalibration within the party away from the culture wars and toward bread-and-butter economic issues, he said.

"It'd be the best thing that could happen to them," Glenn predicted. "I don't see any change occurring in the Republican Party unless they get their ass whipped in November."

Back at the saloon in Houston, after Abbott concluded his remarks, a long line of fans waited to snap a photo with him before being rushed aside by an attentive staffer.

Standing on the outskirts of the crowd stood a retired rancher from the border town of Brownsville, a longtime Republican in a family of other longtime Republicans who cast a ballot as soon as the polls opened. Asked about recent polls showing Hinojosa within a few points of Abbott, the rancher, who declined to share his name, dismissed them as "driven by Democrats."

And questioned about how he thinks his party will fare next week, he shrugged. "It's Texas," he said.

articles.title: Maria Elvira Salazar’s Trump Problem
articles.summary: The Florida Republican is a celebrity in the 305. But suddenly she’s fighting for her political life.
articles.body:
M IAMI — For nearly an hour, dozens of the local Republican Party's most loyal Colombian voters bided their time, piled into a conference room in a small hotel right off the airport near Miami Springs, surrounded by tables full of empanadas, tequeños and small Colombian flags. The event's emcee, Weston City Commissioner Fabio Andrade, in town for the event, hyped up the crowd and warned of a "Machiavellian plan" by Democratic socialists to take over the U.S. He moved about the room, turning the mic to voters one by one.

" Porque apoyan a Maria Elvira?" he asked. Colombians of all ages easily made their case for why they support Maria Elvira Salazar.

" Se faja para el residente, y no para el partido."

She's in favor of immigrants. She defends us Latinos. She works for the residents, not for the party.

A salsa beat came in hot over the speakers. Right on cue, through a backdoor coming off the hotel parking lot, the congresswoman walked in. As if in complete coordination, the group lifted out of their seats and crowded her, whipping out cell phones to snap photos of her rapturous entrance. Sporting a white campaign shirt and white Golden Goose sneakers, her signature blowout slightly puffy from the excess humidity, Salazar was greeted like a celebrity.

"I wish Washington would welcome me with this, and with this music!" she told the small crowd, taking her seat and signaling to one of her aides to grab her a water bottle. More members of her team funneled in, along with Toby, Salazar's small but feisty King Charles Spaniel.

The room quieted as she launched into a passionate defense of what has become her core policy proposal, the Dignity Act — the immigration reform measure that has put her at odds with President Donald Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement. Not long after, an older woman named Beatriz Parga, clad head to toe in red with a "TRUMP 2024" hat, stood and grabbed a mic: is the Dignity Act actually a mass amnesty?

No, Salazar interjected quickly. It's not.

"Son ilegales y se quedaron, es verdad," she said. They came illegally and they stayed. But, Salazar pleaded, " vamos a hacer algo salomónico." Let's do something Solomonic.

"Trump could be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism," Salazar told the crowd, a pitch she's given so many times it's become a cliché.

For decades, Maria Elvira Salazar has been a rock star of the 305. A veteran of Spanish language television, her name has become synonymous with the Cuban American conservative tradition that provides one of the Republican Party's most reliable bases of support. She's a "Cuban Lauren Bacall," as GOP strategist Giancarlo Sopo put it, so personally popular that in 2024 she won more votes in her Miami-based district than President Donald Trump himself.

But in the second Trump era, the forced exodus of thousands of Venezuelans, Colombians, Nicaraguans and even Cubans has upended Miami's immigrant community. It's a policy that stands to unravel the broader GOP coalition that played a key role in Trump's victory — and it's threatening Salazar's political survival.

Interviews with more than two dozen lawmakers, lobbyists, former staffers, GOP operatives, Democratic organizers and Miami voters who know Salazar revealed the extent of the damage to her once-glittering political brand.

Suddenly, she is as despised by some in her party as she is loved. Local Democrats loathe her, viewing Salazar as a hypocrite who has betrayed a vibrant city remade by an explosion of Latino culture and language. Those who support the administration's mass deportation agenda view her as an existential threat to Trump's restrictive immigration policies.

Salazar's predicament is unmistakable in the final days of the midterm campaign. She is facing what appear to be gale force Democratic winds while at the same time navigating the political hazards of one of the GOP's most radioactive issues.

She's privately called James Blair, who heads Trump's political operation, and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, to warn them that the party is at risk of losing Latino voters, she told POLITICO Magazine. "Right now in 2026, the polls are indicating that we may be losing some of that pot of gold if the Republican Party wants to stay in power and continue winning elections," Salazar said.

Neither Blair nor the White House responded to requests for comment.

At the airport hotel event, as the crowd of Colombians swarmed Salazar after her remarks, squeezing up to the front to try and get a selfie with her, Parga held back. Parga told me she still supports Trump, and is a massive fan of Salazar. Yet when asked if she believes the congresswoman will win re-election in November, Parga shrugged. She wasn't sure if voters would show up for her.

"Los cubanos no están con ella," Parga told me. The Cubans aren't with her. But why? "Porque creen que ella no está con Trump," she explained.

They think she's not with the president.

With the clock ticking down toward Election Day, Salazar rolled up on a Wednesday in late September to a pale yellow warehouse off a back alley in Kendall — with a stack of papers and her dog Toby in tow — to record a podcast.

The "Pichy Boys" are two content creators with over one million followers on Instagram. Though not explicitly a political show, the hosts are a mirror of Miami's latest generation of Cubans, delivering their news and hot takes via Reels or TikToks. It's a style of interview the congresswoman has done time and again on the trail this fall — usually friendly, and always with an important Cuban or Venezuelan or Colombian audience that she needs to turn out.

Fixing her hair in the lens of the camera, Salazar appeared to be in her element. The studio had a great setup, she told the hosts. "That's the most important part of a studio — lighting."

If there's one thing to understand about Maria Salazar — core to the signature hair, the color-coordinated outfits, the news anchor posture — it's that she was a fixture of local television for a very long time. That fact is relevant enough that Democrats chose their own veteran local TV personality to oppose her this year: Eliott Rodriguez, a former local news anchor for CBS, who is also Cuban American.

Her media background places her squarely in a tradition of Spanish broadcasting that is the lifeblood of the Cuban exile community in South Florida. Since the first wave of migration from Cuba in the early 1960s — an influx which included Salazar's own family — Cuban-led TV and radio has played an outsized role in Miami. First, it served as a source for exiles to understand what was happening to their families on the island, and for those on the island to get information they weren't hearing from Fidel Castro's revolutionary regime. It was resistance activism as much as it was news.

Born in Miami's Little Havana community just two years after Castro took control of the island, Salazar was part of the next generation of journalists. Univision, CNN en Español, Telemundo and then Mega TV — Salazar was everywhere. Over time, the whole Latino set of the city got to know "Maria Elvira."

"[Salazar] was one of the first people to actually do debate talk shows in Spanish on U.S. television," said a person close to Salazar, granted anonymity to discuss private details. "She's pushy and she's extremely demanding, both with her producers and with her staff. She knows how to throw the zingers, and she's not afraid of controversy. She leans into it."

When Miami's first Cuban representative in Congress, Republican Ileana Ros-Lehtinen, retired in 2018 — opening the seat for the first time in 20 years — Salazar seized the opportunity to leverage her celebrity. She was dragged under by that year's blue wave, but in a rematch two years later with incumbent Democrat and former Cabinet secretary Donna Shalala, she took advantage of presidential year turnout — and the Cuban exile community's affinity for Trump — to capture the seat. Notably, Salazar ran ahead of Trump's performance in her congressional district.

"She was having nightly Zoom shows on Facebook Live with thousands of people, talking about the pandemic," one of her former campaign staffers said. "The cars would stop in the middle of the street and honk and wave her down," when they saw her on the trail. "It all goes back to the fact that she is a journalist and she understands TV extremely well."

It "turned out to be the biggest upset in the country in 2020, because the GOP never really thought, including [former Speaker] Kevin McCarthy, that I could defeat the longest serving member of the Clinton administration with no money from the GOP," Salazar said. "So yeah, miracles happen."

From the moment she took her oath in the Capitol, Salazar wanted to "speak and talk and live and walk immigration," she said in an interview between meetings this week. It formed the crux of her character on the Hill.

In her 2025 book, Dignity Not Citizenship: The Truth About Immigration No One Is Telling You , she described herself as a freshman "with a mission, not to mention a minority woman with a Sofia Vergara accent, who spoke loudly and waved her arms around to drive home a point."

She quickly made allies of her fellow Miami Cuban lawmakers. "There is a difference between, you know, being a journalist and getting into this crazy process," Republican Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart said.

"Her work ethic is just outstanding," he added, calling Salazar "exceedingly intense."

The expansive laws crafted to facilitate the settling of Cubans in the U.S. have always made them an exception among immigrant groups. Yet Salazar was convinced that the next wave of Latinos that came flocking to South Florida in the 2000's weren't as fortunate. So she formed the beginnings of a framework that could legalize the swaths of immigrants who had moved without papers to the U.S. decades ago, but had never gotten status. She called it the Dignity Plan.

Together with Democratic Rep. Veronica Escobar of Texas, she pushed to establish a new "dignity" status for immigrants who'd been living in the U.S. for years, where they would never be eligible for a green card and would agree to pay thousands of dollars in fines. Salazar argues that the bill would clear backlogs in the courts, help immigrants to fill gaps in the workforce and secure the Southern border.

Escobar remembers that when they first met, she was "not a fan" of Salazar.

"She said, 'You need to do something about immigration,' and just started laying into me. And I remember just thinking, 'Who the hell does she think she is to walk up and confront me in this way?'" Escobar said.

But the Texas Democrat also acknowledged that only Salazar came to mind when she looked for a Republican to partner with on a bipartisan immigration proposal.

"She has determination that is almost superhuman," Escobar said. "She is different from a number of legislators that I've worked with over the years, in that respect that she is almost relentless to a point of obsession."

But the latter years of the Biden administration saw an immigration crisis that completely shifted the calculus in Congress. A constant stream of headlines about caravans of immigrants entering through the Southern border inflamed a Republican Party that already viewed the president as dangerously lax on immigration policy.

To them, Salazar's bill amounted to a "mass amnesty" that would worsen an already chaotic situation on the border. And with the GOP taking control of the House in 2023, it was a complete nonstarter.

It wasn't just Salazar's Republican colleagues in Washington who were enraged by the idea of letting in more immigrants. Back in Miami, Cuban Republicans — the oldest of whom had spent half their lives in the U.S., by that point — were also convinced the influx had to stop. Nicaraguan, Colombian and Venezuelan immigrants, the ones who had become U.S. citizens, were thinking the same thing.

Those frustrations helped power Trump, who was promising the "largest deportation program of criminals" in American history, to a sweeping victory in Miami-Dade County in 2024. More than two-thirds of Cubans voted for him.

Salazar, who had campaigned against the chaos at the border and messaged her immigration reform proposal as a tool for shutting the border, won re-election by an even greater margin — 20 points.

Just two years later, however, Miami — and Salazar's winning coalition — is at risk of fracturing.

Away from the loud, music-filled storefronts of Little Havana's Calle Ocho , the tourists looking for coffee and the older Cubans loyal to their game tables at Domino Park, the surrounding neighborhood remains one of the last real working or middle class enclaves of Salazar's district. And amid relics of Spanish architecture and sprawling murals of the Cuban flag, the streets are largely quiet these days.

Almost everyone has a story of someone they know who left out of fear of ICE. Ask your Uber driver to take you to Little Havana, or to Doral, a small immigrant-dominated city outside Salazar's district known as Doral- zuela , and many will flat out tell you no. They can't risk being stopped in their car there. It's a level of fear, of frustration, of wariness, that's unlike anything residents have experienced here — I grew up here, and felt it myself when I returned to report for this story.

"They're treating everyone like criminals, but we built Miami," Martha Cabrera, a Cuban canvasser with the UNITE Here local 355 chapter, told me while knocking doors.

I told her that Salazar was born in this neighborhood. "It seems like she forgot," responded Martha, who was doorbelling for an independent offshoot that has backed Eliott Rodriguez.

The shadow cast by federal immigration enforcement and the detention sweeps has been impossible to avoid. As mass ICE detentions swept the country in 2025 and plunged major cities into protest, Miami registered the highest number of ICE arrests of any field office. That included Cubans — who for much of Miami's recent history were thought to be untouchable. The converging factors of existing city agreements to cooperate with ICE enforcement, and the sudden termination of status for hundreds of thousands of immigrants, living and working in Miami legally under Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation, created a perfect storm for removals. Nearby loomed the makeshift detention center established by Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. Dubbed "Alligator Alcatraz" for its location near the Everglades, the facility was widely condemned for inhumane detention conditions until it was shut down in June.

"The word is decepcionado, " explained Ana Sofia Pelaez, a local activist and executive director of the Miami Freedom Project, when asked how Latino voters felt about the detention policies. "In English it can mean you were deceived or you were just disappointed." In Spanish, it means both.

In D.C., Salazar started sounding the alarm about what she was hearing back home. Latino voters were angry, she told her colleagues. The indiscriminate enforcement wasn't what they voted for. Her Miami Republican colleagues, from Diaz-Balart and Carlos Gimenez to local Republicans, raised the same red flags.

She warned GOP leadership that if the enforcement continued, they would lose Latino voters in the midterms. "That's a mistake that is going to cost us dearly, and I've been telling my Trump administration. I've been telling ICE," she told reporters in July.

She explained to fellow House Republicans that, thanks to Trump, the Southern border was now closed. She saw an opening for the Dignity Act, which she had re-introduced along with Escobar in 2025.

"I'm trying to make the GOP the party that will send the message to the Hispanics that they're welcomed and that they have the same values that are entrenched in the Republican Party: God-fearing, law-abiding, tax-paying, good people, hard workers," Salazar said. "They are here, so let's just give them dignity so they can stay."

Instead, she found herself in what she called a "two-front war": Democrats wouldn't work with her without the promise of a path to citizenship, and many Republicans simply rejected her plan outright.

In fact, top administration allies, key Trump confidants and Salazar's own GOP colleagues on the Hill lead the charge against the measure. "The Dignity Act is mass amnesty and would constitute a terrible betrayal of our voters," Republican Rep. Brandon Gill of Texas, one of the bill's biggest critics, wrote on X . One of her Florida delegation colleagues, Republican Rep. Randy Fine, wrote on X that it "should never see the light of day" in the House.

Several far-right advocates came together to form a Mass Deportation Coalition at the height of the backlash, and some formed a PAC to specifically attack "pro-amnesty" candidates who backed the Dignity Act .

The congresswoman is "first and foremost, an ethno-lobbyist," said Mike Howell of the Mass Deportation Coalition.

"What are you doing here, Maria Salazar? Go join the other party," he added. "How can the president endorse somebody who is boldly opposing his central thesis?"

Mark Krikorian, executive director of the right-leaning Center for Immigration Studies, called the proposal "so preposterous" that the party shouldn't even engage with it. Even if it was viable, Krikorian said, Salazar should not be the face of it because "she's incredibly obnoxious and aggressive, and turns off people even on our own side."

Salazar said she received death threats for her departure from MAGA orthodoxy. There were calls for her to be primaried. "I don't want the Republicans to lose the House, but at this point in time, like, what's the difference between Maria Salazar and a Democrat?" Laura Loomer told POLITICO back in April.

Democrats have been just as hard on her, for voting along party lines to allocate billions of dollars to the agency behind the ICE detention sweeps, the Homeland Security Department.

"Maybe at one time she was known as a tough journalist and someone who could be trusted, but by now people know her as a politician who cannot be trusted and who doesn't tell the truth," Rodriguez, Salazar's Democratic opponent, told POLITICO Magazine. "She votes with MAGA all the time, and they're not fooled by it."

Caught between two pincers, Salazar went back to her roots in September: She got on TV. This time, with a message for Trump himself.

Standing in front of the White House, speaking directly to the camera, Salazar told the president that "some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far." The campaign ad went on: "Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy … The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

In Miami, almost no one was surprised by the spot. But back in Washington, it hit like a political earthquake, a rare rebuke of a president who tolerates no dissent from the party line. The video went viral, racking up millions of views.

"I wanted him to hear directly from me," Salazar said. "[I was] not attacking him. I was forewarning him."

"He's a construction and hospitality guy. He's a businessman. He is the one to fix this 40-year problem," she added.

To the far-right — the "America First" believers in Trump's campaign promises — her position had already represented an "existential threat" to the future of the Republican Party. But the ad? Name-checking the president? Right in front of the White House? It crossed a line.

Angry callers inundated Miami's Cuban radio shows, phoning in to say Salazar went too far. Ninoska Pérez Castellón, host at "La Poderosa" and one of the giants of the Cuban conservative airwaves, was among the radio hosts fielding the calls. Whoever wrote the ad, she said, did Salazar "un gran mal" — a disservice.

"She could have said the same thing without using the language that she used," Pérez Castellón said. "The word she used is 'betrayed.' That [Trump] 'betrayed' us. I don't know if I agree."

At first, Trump showed Salazar a little grace. Rather than revoke his endorsement, he told reporters she was a "nice person" who "got a little bit soft on the border."

Then he had a change of heart. He re-shared a series of Truth Social posts attacking her, and in some cases, calling for her replacement.

Sitting at the center of a long table, flanked by the Republican mayors from the southern neighborhoods of her district, Salazar held court on a recent October morning. Hundreds of attendees packed the meeting, from prominent Miami industry reps to regular constituents, all gathered at 7:30 am to meet her at Casa Cuba, a classic South Miami spot.

Grant Miller of Miami Community Newspapers, which hosted the breakfast for Salazar, invited the congresswoman up to the small stage and got down on one knee to hold her stack of papers, not long after joking he would marry her. Donning bright red reading glasses, Salazar without delay launched into her immigration pitch. "I do believe Trump will sign immigration reform law, and it will be Dignity," she told the room. "Once the Dignity Act passes, I will have done my job."

Even in the final stretch of an increasingly competitive — and contentious — race, Salazar has not backed down from the position that has made her a pariah to many in her party. It's made her a test case for whether a Republican can win a majority Latino district in the era of mass deportation.

Outside Casa Cuba, sitting at a tiled table after the breakfast, Ramona Tumon and Mirla Loredo lamented they weren't able to grab a photo with the congresswoman. The pair of friends, both Cuban, moved to Miami in the late 60's. Loredo told me in no uncertain terms: she's not a fan of the Dignity Act and she didn't like Salazar's ad. Tumon, however, did support the proposal. She tried to convince Loredo to no avail.

Both already voted Republican up and down the ballot, including for Salazar. Why vote for Salazar, I asked Loredo, if you disagree with her signature policy proposal? She said she didn't want the GOP to lose the House.

Cuban Republicans may be angry with Salazar, Loredo said, but they have to vote GOP in spite of it. " No les queda más remedio," she said. "They don't have another choice."

" Tienen que votar por ella, sino nos toca el otro," Loredo added. "They have to vote for her, or else we get the other guy," referring to Rodriguez.

Salazar remains a slight favorite to win. She has significantly outspent Rodriguez, who has gone through the race without any ads on broadcast TV. He's the beneficiary of a late infusion of support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and an 11th hour spend by the House Majority PAC, but the GOP has a voter registration edge of about 45,000 voters, according to Florida International University's Eduardo Gamarra.

The latest FIU Cuba poll , which has been surveying the community for years, found that 76% of respondents disapprove of the administration's immigration crackdown on Cuban nationals — but 68% of Cubans still plan to vote for the GOP candidate in their district next week.

Yet with significant headwinds buffeting the Republican Party, and Trump's approval rating plummeting, GOP turnout is by no means guaranteed — in Miami or anywhere else. "They're not enthusiastic about going out to the polls," Gamarra said. For many Latino Republicans, "they're not switching parties, and they're just simply not going to show up."

If Republicans do show up on Election Day, said Venezuelan activist Adelys Ferro of Latino Victory, it may be due to the deep loyalty to MAGA that still thrives in Salazar's Cuban base, an affinity rooted in Trump's anti-socialist and law-and-order messaging.

"If she loses," Ferro argued, "it's on her."

Should Salazar win on Tuesday, her problems will be far from over. She'll likely return to Washington as a member of the House minority. A disproportionate number of her Republican Dignity Act co-sponsors may not survive their own re-elections. Trump's final two years have set a hard deadline to make good on Salazar's repeated assurances that he'll sign sweeping immigration reform, but he's given no indication to date that he's willing to buck the MAGA base on the issue.

Salazar has demurred from making any grand predictions about what voters will do on Nov. 3. "I know District Number 27 probably better than anybody," she told reporters after the Casa Cuba event, as a line of constituents formed to get photos with her. "If they think that I've done a good job, they'll bring me back, regardless of the political affiliation."

articles.title: Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm push
articles.summary: But select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to vote
articles.body:
In races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support them have released ads accusing Republicans of protecting pedophiles by voting against legislation to release files related to Jeffrey Epstein .

The ads appear intended to evoke an emotional response by accusing candidates of "protecting" Epstein, a notorious pedophile accused of running a sex-trafficking ring involving minors.

An analysis from CNN found that candidates and outside groups have spent more than $35m on Epstein-related ads. Another from the Washington Post found that Democrats spent more than $40m on Epstein-related ads across six key Senate races.

In Colorado, ads targeting Republican Jeff Crank note that the lawmaker voted against releasing the Epstein files. In one , the family members of Virginia Giuffre, a woman who survived abuse at the hands of Epstein and died by suicide last year, claim Crank "covered up Epstein's crimes to protect Donald Trump".

Ashley Hinson, a Senate candidate in Iowa, was accused of voting to "protect her donors" by refusing to vote to release the Epstein files.

"This week I had to explain to my boys, 'No, Mom does not protect pedophiles,'" Hinson said in a campaign ad responding to attacks over the Epstein files.

An ad targeting Mike Collins , the Republican running for a Georgia Senate seat, says "Mike Collins voted against releasing the Epstein files even after he knew Epstein's sex-trafficking operation exploited 14-year-old girls for sex".

Florida Republican Jimmy Patronis faced an attack from his Democratic opponent, claiming he called investigating Epstein "a waste of his time".

A spokesperson for Crank's campaign accused the Epstein-related ad of being "intentionally vague", in a statement to the Washington Post, because his position was that he would vote against the file's release until he could be confident that victim information was properly redacted. The campaign also said it was "unfortunate" that his opponent, Jessica Killin, was "preying on a grieving family with the help of the Washington Democrats".

Crank's staff invited and met with Giuffre's family, though Crank himself did not meet with them in person, the New York Times reported. Crank's campaign also said it offered to meet with Epstein victims before the vote on the legislation.

Last year, Democrats and a select few House Republicans tried to force a vote on the Epstein files through a discharge petition – a procedure used in Congress to bypass the traditional steps of legislation and force a vote on the House floor.

Donald Trump, who knew Epstein in the 1990s and early 2000s, opposed the discharge petition for the files, reversing his campaign promise to increase government transparency. House Republicans largely aligned themselves with him, prompting anger from high-profile Trump voters.

Eventually, under pressure from allies, Trump supported the legislation, giving Republican lawmakers the go-ahead to vote for it. All but one House Republican voted for the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

Many of the ads omit the fact that nearly every House Republican voted to release the Epstein files when the Epstein Files Transparency Act came to the floor, although at that point Trump had agreed to sign the legislation and release the files. Instead, the ads refer to Republicans opposing early attempts to force the legislation to the floor.

Republicans have pointed to this fact when disputing the attack ads.

"Of course I voted to release the Epstein files," Hinson said in a direct-to-camera ad, accusing her opponent, Josh Turek, of lying. While Hinson voted for the final Epstein Files Transparency Act, she did not sign on to the discharge petition.

Patronis, meanwhile, never called the investigation a "waste of time", but told a local radio station that while he had "no problem getting everything all released", the issue was a "massive energy and time suck at the end of the day".

Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for Patronis's campaign, highlighted his work with Trump to obtain disaster funding after Hurricane Isaias and said his opponent, Gay Valimont, was "still talking about a dead pedophile in a sad web video than helping the people of [the first congressional district] recover."

Some Republicans and groups supporting the GOP have sought to flip the script, accusing Democrats of taking money from donors who had ties to Epstein.

During a Georgia Senate debate, Collins accused his opponent, Jon Ossoff, of accepting campaign donations from Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire who had ties to Epstein. Hoffman has said he only knew Epstein through fundraising relationships and regrets it.

"You can claim to fight against the Epstein class, but I'm going to tell you, this call is coming from inside the house and the Epstein class is on stage right now and it's you," Collins said .

In New Mexico's gubernatorial race, an outside group released an ad accusing Democratic candidate Deb Haaland of accepting a ride on Epstein's private jet and taking "tens of thousands of dollars from Epstein businesses" and then "asking for more".

Haaland did not fly on Epstein's jet, but did take a flight booked by one of Epstein's companies in 2014. Haaland has said she was unaware the chartered flight was owned by an Epstein-owned company.

articles.title: El-Sayed drops Stevens from campaign event
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) told Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), his once primary opponent, to stay away from his campaign events and disinvit...
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) told Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), his once primary opponent, to stay away from his campaign events and disinvited her from a planned appearance on Sunday, a source familiar confirmed to NewsNation, The Hill's broadcasting partner.

The source said El-Sayed does not want the ongoing fight with Stevens to distract from the issues in the final days of his hard-fought Senate campaign.

A spokesperson for Stevens did not immediately respond to The Hill's request for comment.

El-Sayed was set to appear alongside Stevens and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) at a church in Detroit, a show of unity despite some harsh words exchanged between the two candidates throughout the week.

Stevens released a statement saying she had accepted Clyburn's invitation to appear alongside El-Sayed, but still criticized the Senate nominee for not condemning an ad that appeared to blame Israel for high grocery prices.

"The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and child care," Stevens said in her statement. "I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well."

The ad was run digitally and was bought by an outside progressive group, not El-Sayed's campaign.

El-Sayed shot back in a statement on Friday, saying Stevens is focused on rehashing their August primary, which he narrowly won.

"So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let's all focus on the task at hand: that's beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics," El-Sayed said in a statement posted to the social platform X.

Support for Israel was a major issue in the Democratic primary. Stevens was backed by millions in funds from pro-Israel lobbying groups, which El-Sayed criticized her for. The Democratic Senate nominee is critical of Israel and has called for the U.S. to stop sending aid to the country.

Since the primary, courting Jewish voters has been a hurdle for El-Sayed. His Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has worked to earn the support of disaffected Democrats, including those who are Jewish.

While Stevens told CNN this week that she still plans to vote for El-Sayed, her fiancé, who is Jewish, announced that he would be voting for Rogers.

articles.title: At Balachaur rally, Saini pitches BJP’s 2027 Punjab return
articles.summary: Haryana CM Nayab Singh Saini says BJP will form Punjab govt in Feb 2027; targets AAP and Congress over drugs, jobs; urges youth to shun drugs.
articles.body: Chandigarh: Haryana chief minister Nayab Singh Saini on Saturday projected the BJP as the alternative to AAP and Congress in Punjab, asserting that a govt under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership would be formed in the state in Feb 2027.Addressing a youth rally at Bagowal village in Balachaur constituency, Saini accused successive governments of failing to tackle Punjab’s drug crisis and provide employment to young people. He urged the youth to stay away from drugs, pursue their ambitions and contribute to the development of their villages and society.During the event, activist Ravi Inder Singh Balachaur joined the BJP along with several associates. Welcoming them, Saini assured them of respect and recognition within the party.The CM said Punjab was passing through a difficult phase, with drugs destroying families and holding back development. He accused Congress of failing to fulfil its promise to eradicate drugs and AAP of reneging on its commitments to eliminate drug abuse and provide employment to 25 lakh youth. Claiming that the AAP government had failed to deliver on its promises despite setting deadlines to eradicate drugs, Saini alleged that it had proved more corrupt than Congress and was registering cases against those who spoke out against drug sales.Calling for a ‘Rangla Punjab’, he said every child should have access to a playground, every youth an opportunity to progress and every family support against drugs. The BJP’s anti-drug yatra had received public support, he claimed, adding that improving rural sports stadiums and promoting sports would help keep young people away from drugs.Saini urged youth to dream big but not be compelled by circumstances to migrate abroad or take the ‘dunki route’. articles.title: Daylight saving time is almost over. Here's what to know.
articles.summary: Millions of Americans gain an hour of sleep this weekend when the time change commonly known as daylight savings ends for 2026, meaning clocks "fall back."
articles.body:
Millions of Americans will gain an hour of sleep this weekend when the twice-a-year time change commonly known as daylight savings ends for 2026. Most of the U.S. will "fall back" an hour when the clocks change at 2 a.m. on Sunday.

Here's what to know about what's formally known as daylight saving time as it ends for the year:

What is daylight saving time, and why do we have it?

Daylight saving time is the period during the year, from March to early November, when the majority of the U.S. operates one hour ahead of standard time.

The move effectively "saves" an hour of daylight from the morning and adds it to the evening during the spring and summer months when the days are the longest. In the fall and winter months, when the days are shorter, the U.S. returns to standard time, with daylight coming earlier in the morning.

For example, in Boston on Saturday, before the time change, the sun will rise at 7:16 a.m. and set at 5:39 p.m., according to the National Weather Service . On Sunday, back on standard time, sunrise will be at 6:17 a.m. and sunset will be at 4:37 p.m.

The U.S. first adopted daylight saving time in 1918 during World War I as an effort to conserve fuel after Europe implemented its own time change, according to the Congressional Research Service . After the war, Congress repealed the clock switch but gave states the option to continue observing it.

During World War II and the 1970s energy crisis, Congress brought year-round daylight saving time to the U.S., again with the goal of reducing energy consumption. These experiments didn't last long.

After the war, the U.S. let states and municipalities decide for themselves if they wanted to keep daylight saving time and when to observe it. (Congress didn't establish a uniform start and end for the time change until 1966.) In the '70s, continuous daylight saving time was stopped before reaching the 10-month mark.

Will the U.S. move to year-round daylight saving time?

Earlier this year, legislation to once again make daylight saving time last all year long cleared a major hurdle in Congress. The bill, called the Sunshine Protection Act, passed the House in July and went to the Senate . The legislation would also let states opt out of daylight saving time altogether before the law takes effect.

President Trump, who supports the bill, accused a fellow Republican, Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, of holding up the legislation . Mr. Trump even posted to social media what he said was Cotton's cellphone number and urged people to call the senator to express their support for the measure.

In response, Cotton noted Congress has tried permanent daylight saving time before, only to go back to the twice-yearly time change "once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter."

There is a ticking clock for the Senate to take action on the bill. The legislation and any other bills awaiting approval in Congress are set to expire in early January when the new class of lawmakers elected in Tuesday's midterm elections takes office.

If the bill does die, the effort to change daylight saving time will have to start over and be approved by the House and the Senate before it can go to the president.

For 2026, the end of daylight saving time comes during the overnight hours after Halloween, giving revelers an extra hour of enjoying late-night costume parties — or an extra hour of sleep to recover from their fun.

But for parents of young children, the time change can be more of a trick and less of a treat, potentially disrupting their kids' sleep schedules until they adjust.

What day and time does daylight saving time end in November 2026?

Daylight saving time officially ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, Nov. 1.

Americans have been "falling back" on the first Sunday of November since 2007, when the most recent changes to daylight saving time took effect . A 2005 law moved the end date from the last Sunday of October.

Do we lose or gain an hour when daylight saving time ends?

Most Americans will gain an hour when daylight saving time ends, making up for the hour they lost when the clocks "sprang forward" in March.

When will daylight saving time start again in 2027?

Daylight saving time is set to begin in 2027 on Sunday, March 14, at 2 a.m. local time. The time change starts on the second Sunday of March, which falls on such a late date next year because the month starts on a Monday. In 2026, daylight saving time started on March 8 .

The start date was also changed in 2007 to extend the length of daylight saving time, which previously began on the first Sunday of April.

Which states don't do daylight saving time?

Daylight saving time is observed in every state except for Hawaii and most of Arizona . The Navajo Nation, which is located in part of Arizona, observes the time change to stay on the same time as their communities in the neighboring states of New Mexico and Utah, according to the tribe .

The U.S. territories of American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands also don't observe daylight saving time.

Will my phone change for daylight saving time automatically?

Phones should change overnight to display the correct time if they're set to update automatically.

Apple , Google and Samsung have support pages with instructions for changing the clocks on their devices. Carriers like Simple Mobile and Straight Talk have also posted steps online for checking the settings on other phones.

articles.title: Ramaswamy among nearly $700K in donations for harassed Red Baron worker
articles.summary: An online fundraiser for a Red Baron Pizza employee in Michigan raised nearly $700,000 after the man was targeted in a viral online prank. The nearly 20,000 donations on GoFundMe include a $38,000 from Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (R) and his wife Apoorva, his campaign confirmed to The Hill Saturday. In a viral video…
articles.body:
An online fundraiser for a Red Baron Pizza employee in Michigan raised nearly $700,000 after the man was targeted in a viral online prank.

The nearly 20,000 donations on GoFundMe include a $38,000 from Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (R) and his wife Apoorva, his campaign confirmed to The Hill Saturday.

In a viral video shared on social media, a man approaches the Red Baron employee, named Walt, with his cell phone. He holds it up to Walt and plays the sound emitted by an Apple device when making a purchase with Apple Pay, telling the employee that he just charged him $10 — but no funds are actually debited.

The stunt is part of an online trend where an individual approaches someone and pretends to charge them using mobile payment to elicit a reaction.

“It’s not a joke to me, okay? I don’t have time for this crap in my life, my life is hard enough as it is,” Walt said in the video. “Now I’m probably going to get kicked out of the store because of you … You’re probably making money off of this, and I can’t even pay my God—- mortgage, and I got four kids at home.”

Ramaswamy shared his support for Walt in a post to the social platform X.

“A hardworking dad with a mortgage & kids at home, struggling to make ends meet for his family. There are millions of Ohioans just like him & that’s who we’re fighting for,” Ramaswamy wrote. “We’re behind you, Walt.”

Walt’s fears of losing his job did not come to fruition either — Red Baron announced that he is their employee of the month.

“Employee of the month nominations are closed. You know why,” the company wrote in a post on X.

Walt responded on the GoFundMe page, thanking the donors and sharing the joy it has brought him and his family.

“My wife and I have been reading your posts and comments, and we’ve gone from being deeply moved to laughing until we can barely breathe. Some of you are seriously funny. I wasn’t expecting a comedy show in the middle of all this, but apparently the internet had other plans,” he wrote.

“I’m still finding my footing with all this attention, so bear with me,” he added. “My wife and I are also trying to keep everyday life steady for our kids. They didn’t sign up for an audience, and being their dad comes first.”

articles.title: Veteran Dem operative says subpar GOP candidates poised to hand over Senate majority
articles.summary: Dan Turrentine says poor Republican candidate quality in Texas, Mississippi, Kansas and Ohio could hand Democrats full Senate control on Tuesday.

Dan Turrentine, who served as chief of staff to current Colorado Gov. Jared Polis when he was a member of Congress, said several close Senate races seem to be trending Democrat in the leadup to Tuesday's election. "Five days out, Democrats have a pretty good chance to retake the Senate," Turrentine said. He cited several races, including North Carolina, where incumbent Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is retiring. That seat, which has long been red, seems poised to flip as polls show former Gov. Roy Cooper holds a commanding lead over former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley. SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY Republicans, who are widely projected to lose their slim House majority, currently hold a 53-47 lead in the Senate. In addition to North Carolina, a number of surprisingly close Senate races in both swing states like Ohio and Michigan, and in typically deep red states such as Texas, Kansas and Missouri, have Democrats like Turrentine hopeful they can gain full control of Congress on Tuesday. While crediting smart campaigning from Democrats, Turrentine also pinned Republican shortcomings on what he called poor candidate quality. He cited Ken Paxton in Texas, Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, Roger Marshall in Kansas and Darlene Graham Nordone, who is running to take the seat of her late brother, former Sen. Lindsey Graham. GOP SENATE MAJORITY FACES FRESH UNCERTAINTY AS 2 KEY RACES TIGHTEN DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS "If Republicans lose the Senate, it’s likely one of those four loses," said Turrentine, who hosts "The Huddle" podcast with former White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: SOUTH CAROLINA MOVES TO TOSS-UP But while Democrats are performing well in polls, Turrentine acknowledged that previous surveys have overstated support for his party. THE SILENT MAJORITY PROBLEM AND WHY CAMPAIGN POLLSTERS KEEP 'FIGHTING THE LAST WAR' ON ELECTIONS "We’ve had consecutive change elections — 2016, 2022, 2024 — where polling struggled to capture late-breaking dynamics. Will frustrated Trump voters stay home, or will early Democratic surges in Texas just reflect high-propensity voters banking votes early rather than expanding the electorate? Nobody knows, and people have a knot in their stomach about Tuesday," he said.
